analysis.one_liner: Tightens pollution limits on fossil-fuel power plants, including a cap on carbon dioxide emissions.
analysis.headline: The Clean Power Plant Act of 1999 never got a vote: after being sent to five House committees, it sat in subcommittees for over a year until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every fossil-fuel power plant in the country — including old plants that had been exempt from modern clean air rules — to meet strict limits on mercury, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and carbon dioxide starting in 2005. It included a carbon dioxide cap-and-trade system, public disclosure of each plant's emissions to consumers, and billions of dollars in aid for coal workers and coal-dependent towns. It never received a hearing or a vote in any committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people living downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants, whose air would carry less fine particulate matter, smog, acid rain, and mercury. The bill's own findings cite fine particulates associated with roughly 50,000 American deaths annually and mercury contamination that makes fish unsafe to eat, especially for pregnant women [S3]. Electricity consumers would gain from required disclosure of each plant's emissions [S3]. Coal and oil workers facing job losses and towns losing plant tax revenue would receive retraining and economic development aid funded by the bill [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires every fossil-fuel generating unit of 15 megawatts or more to meet strict emission limits for mercury, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen oxides, closing the 'grandfather' loophole that exempted older plants built before the Clean Air Act standards applied — 77% of the 1,000 largest emitting units were exempt under then-current law [S3].

Caps total carbon dioxide emissions from large fossil-fuel plants through a generation performance standard with tradable allowances, a $100-per-ton excess emissions penalty, and continuous monitoring [S2,S3].
Requires plant owners to report emissions quarterly and to disclose to residential customers on a regular basis the emissions levels of the electricity they are buying [S3].

Authorizes $75 million per year for 15 years to retrain coal and oil workers displaced by reduced coal use, another $75 million per year for economic development in affected communities, and property tax relief grants for towns that lose a plant providing 20% or more of their tax base [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal- and oil-fired power plants, who would bear the cost of installing pollution controls or retiring old units, and by extension their customers and shareholders through higher electricity prices or stranded assets. The coal mining and coal transportation industries would face reduced demand as dirtier plants shut down or switched fuels. The federal budget would absorb roughly $1.5 billion per year in authorized worker, community, and research spending [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal-fired plant owners and coal communities

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs would fall on utilities and would likely be passed at least partly to electricity customers through rates, and the bill authorized large federal spending — $75 million per year each for worker assistance and community development for 15 years, plus research funding — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

Coal-dependent regions could see job losses and eroded local tax bases; the bill itself concedes this by including worker retraining, community development aid, and property tax relief for towns where plants close [S2,S3].

The carbon dioxide allowance trading system permits plants to exceed the emissions standard if they buy sufficient credits, and utilities would earn credits for early retirements in any future climate program, provisions that soften the cap's bite [S2,S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental benefits — fewer particulate deaths, less smog and mercury, a first-ever cap on power plant carbon dioxide — are large and broad, while the costs concentrate on a specific industry and on coal-dependent towns, for which the bill provides dedicated transition aid. The design is reasonably serious: it pairs mandates with worker and community assistance and consumer disclosure. Its main weakness is that the carbon cap relies partly on allowance trading, which lets some plants keep emitting if they pay.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to five different House committees, then parked in subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Allen introduced the bill on September 30, 1999, with 18 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Banking and Financial Services, and Science committees [S1,S3,S5].
It was ultimately referred to five committees and then to five subcommittees between October 1 and October 25, 1999 [S5].
The bill gathered 31 cosponsors — 29 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent — but received no hearings, no markup, and no floor action [S4,S5].
Its last recorded action was a second round of sponsor remarks on the House floor on October 4, 2000, a year after introduction; the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5,S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of old coal- and oil-fired power plants, who avoided the cost of modern pollution controls and a carbon cap for another four years, and the coal industry, which faced no new demand shock. The public did not get the emissions cuts the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-fired plant owners and the coal industry

for.name: Rep. Thomas Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Power Plant Act of 1999 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor twice, in 1999 and 2000

for.name: 31 House cosponsors

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it nominal bipartisan support but no committee traction

against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out or scheduled a markup during the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The 31 cosponsors were almost entirely Democrats (29 of 31, with 1 Republican and 1 Independent), and no committee chaired by either party ever brought the bill to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would force old grandfathered plants to install modern pollution controls and buy carbon allowances, with a $100-per-ton penalty for exceeding them. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran against the public's interest in cleaner air and a lower-carbon power supply.

Reduced coal consumption by power plants would cut demand for coal; the bill acknowledged this by funding worker retraining and community development for coal-dependent regions. Blocking the bill preserved the industry's existing market.

industries.industry: Pollution control and clean energy technology makers
industries.note: The bill cites fluidized bed combustion, gasification, flue gas controls, renewables, and fuel cells as the compliance path, and funds carbon sequestration research. Compliance demand would flow to these industries.

industries.industry: Publicly owned coal towns and displaced coal workers
industries.note: Plant retirements would cost jobs and property tax revenue, but the bill dedicates $75 million per year for worker retraining and community economic development, plus property tax relief grants. These constituencies both lose from the cleanup and gain from the transition aid.
